messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Amir is a 64-year-old divorced Middle Eastern man who spent years working as a relief coordinator in a war-torn region. His most traumatic memory is of a night when an airstrike hit a school he had converted into a shelter. He had been distributing food when the building collapsed around him. He remembers the smell—burnt wiring, dust, and flesh—before he even heard the screams. Now, decades later, he is a politician in a Midwestern city, and that smell still finds him. A passing car’s exhaust, a neighbor’s grill, the faint tang of smoke from a distant fire—each one can send him back to that moment. When that happens, the memory returns in fragmented pieces: the sound of a wall groaning, a child’s shoe in the rubble, the heat on his face. He feels the same terror he felt then, so overwhelming that he has to stop whatever he is doing.

Amir has learned to manage these intrusions. When he talks to strangers at fundraising dinners or town halls, he notices his heart racing. He tells himself to stay calm, to control his emotions, and he distracts himself by focusing on the next person in line. But the effort is exhausting. He has thrown himself into work, taking on extra committees and late-night meetings, because keeping his mind occupied keeps the memories at bay. Yet the silence of an empty office after hours feels dangerous to him. He has come to believe that unusual silence means something terrible is about to happen. He constantly scans his surroundings for signs of danger—a door left ajar, a shadow in the hallway, a car idling too long outside the building. Before leaving his house each morning, he repeatedly checks that the doors and windows are locked, sometimes three or four times.

The causal loops have tightened over the years. When a trigger—like a stranger’s comment about military action—brings the memory rushing back, Amir’s sense of threat spikes. He becomes hypervigilant, scanning the room for exits, and his need to control his emotions intensifies. He will excuse himself, go to the bathroom, and breathe slowly until the feeling passes. But the very act of controlling his emotions, of pushing the memory down, seems to make the next intrusion more vivid. The more he distracts himself, the more the memory returns in disconnected, terrifying pieces. And each time he checks a lock or scans a crowd, he is reminded of the fragility of safety, which in turn makes the memory feel more present and more dangerous.

His divorce, years ago, was partly a casualty of this cycle. His wife could not understand why he would freeze during a dinner party when someone mentioned the news, or why he insisted on checking the locks before they went to bed. He could not explain it to her—he barely understood it himself. Now he lives alone, and his adult children worry about him. He has told them he is fine, but he knows he is not. What finally brought him to seek help was a moment at a city council meeting last month. A colleague made a joke about the smell of burnt coffee in the break room, and Amir had to leave the room, shaking, his heart pounding so hard he thought he might collapse. He sat in his car for twenty minutes, trying to breathe, certain that something terrible was about to happen. He is afraid that if he does not get control of this, he will lose his career the way he lost his marriage. But what he is most afraid of is that the memory will never stop feeling like it is happening right now.
